chief_complaint: 6 months of excessive, uncontrollable worry about everyday routines with muscle tension, insomnia, and GAD-7 score 15
hpi_details: 34M presents with 6 months of excessive, difficult-to-control worry about everyday matters — his job performance, finances, and his family's health — occurring more days than not. He reports associated muscle tension, feeling constantly 'on edge,' difficulty concentrating, and trouble falling asleep due to racing thoughts. He has started avoiding coffee because it worsens his jitteriness. Denies discrete panic attacks, palpitations, or episodes of chest tightness. Denies any thoughts of self-harm. He has never taken medication or seen a therapist for this before.
ideas: thinks he might just be a chronic worrier but it's starting to affect his daily life
concerns: He is worried that his constant agitation will cause him to make a costly mistake at work or snap at his loved ones.
expectations: He hopes to get a full physical checkup to rule out a bodily problem and learn practical strategies to calm his racing mind.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Generalized Anxiety Disorder evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Generalized Anxiety Disorder is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management for Generalized Anxiety Disorder emphasizes first-line SSRI or SNRI pharmacotherapy combined with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, with benzodiazepines avoided as routine therapy given their dependence and withdrawal risk.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: 6 months of excessive, uncontrollable worry about everyday routines with muscle tension, insomnia, and GAD-7 score 15

Key HPI features: 34M presents with 6 months of excessive, difficult-to-control worry about everyday matters — his job performance, finances, and his family's health — occurring more days than not. He reports associated muscle tension, feeling constantly 'on edge,' difficulty concentrating, and trouble falling asleep due to racing thoughts. He has started avoiding coffee because it worsens his jitteriness. Denies discrete panic attacks, palpitations, or episodes of chest tightness. Denies any thoughts of self-harm. He has never taken medication or seen a therapist for this before.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 82, BP 128/80, Temp 36.8C. Physical exam unremarkable: no tremor, no exophthalmos, no thyromegaly or thyroid nodules, regular rhythm without resting tachycardia. Mental status exam: appears mildly restless and fidgety, mood 'anxious,' affect congruent, speech normal rate, thought process linear without evidence of psychosis, no suicidal or homicidal ideation. GAD-7 anxiety screen score: 15/21 (severe anxiety). Baseline TSH ordered to exclude hyperthyroidism as a mimicking/contributing cause.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hyperthyroidism (should be screened) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Suicidal ideation or a specific plan — needs urgent psychiatric evaluation and safety assessment.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis using DSM-5 criteria (excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple domains for 6+ months, with at least 3 associated symptoms: restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance) and exclude medical mimics (hyperthyroidism, caffeine/stimulant excess, substance withdrawal) with a baseline TSH.

Initiate first-line pharmacotherapy with an SSRI (e.g., Escitalopram 10 mg PO daily, titrating as tolerated) or an SNRI, counseling that full response may take 4-6 weeks and starting at a low dose to minimize initial jitteriness/activation.
Refer for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, which is equally effective to medication and provides durable long-term symptom control and relapse prevention.

Avoid routine use of benzodiazepines for ongoing management given their risk of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal; reserve short, time-limited courses only for severe acute distress while awaiting SSRI/SNRI onset, with a clear taper plan.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.plan: 1. Order baseline TSH to exclude hyperthyroidism as a contributing/mimicking cause. 2. Initiate first-line SSRI pharmacotherapy: Escitalopram 5 mg PO daily for 1 week, then titrating to 10 mg daily, counseling that full response may take 4-6 weeks. 3. Refer for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy. 4. Provide sleep hygiene counseling and recommend reducing caffeine intake. 5. Avoid routine benzodiazepine prescribing given dependence risk; reassess in 2-4 weeks to track GAD-7 score and side effects.

teaching.one_liner: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about everyday matters for at least six months, accompanied by muscle tension and insomnia — managed with an SSRI and CBT, avoiding benzodiazepines to prevent dependence.
red_flags: Suicidal ideation or a specific plan — needs urgent psychiatric evaluation and safety assessment
Tremor, tachycardia, heat intolerance, or unintentional weight loss — hyperthyroidism can mimic or worsen anxiety and must be excluded
Panic attacks with chest pain or palpitations — cardiac causes must be excluded before attributing symptoms to anxiety

must_ask.say: What kinds of things do you find yourself worrying about, and can you control it?
Do you have muscle tension or trouble falling asleep?
How many months has this been going on?
How is this affecting your work or relationships?
Have you tried anything to manage this, like medication or alcohol?

history.answer: I've been feeling constantly anxious and worrying way too much about everyday things for the past six months.
I'm really worried that I'll lose my temper with my family or mess up a big project at work because my head won't stop spinning.
It started about six months ago, and I have felt this excessive worry more days than not ever since.
The worry is steady and present throughout most of the day; I do not get sudden, intense surges of panic that peak within minutes.
No, I don't get sudden heart pounding, severe shortness of breath, chest tightness, or a feeling that I'm about to die.
I don't avoid specific places or fear leaving home; the worry just follows me wherever I go.
I feel some normal nervousness before public presentations, but my anxiety isn't centered around social situations or fear of being judged.
My neck and shoulder muscles feel tight and achy all the time, and I constantly feel restless and on edge.
I get worn out very easily during the day, and it's hard to concentrate because worrisome thoughts keep interrupting my mind.
I have a really hard time falling asleep at night because my thoughts just keep racing about what could go wrong.
It is making me less productive at my job, and I struggle to be present and relax with my family.
There hasn't been a single major crisis; it's ordinary daily responsibilities that feel overwhelmingly stressful to me.
No, I haven't been through any traumatic events, and I don't have nightmares, flashbacks, or repetitive rituals I feel forced to repeat.
I feel stressed and worn down by the anxiety, but I'm not feeling depressed and I have never had any thoughts of hurting myself or suicide.
No, I haven't lost weight, I don't feel unusually sensitive to heat, and I don't have excessive sweating.
No, I never have chest pain, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness when exercising, and I have never passed out.
I used to drink two cups of coffee a day, but I stopped drinking it completely because it made my jitteriness worse.
I don't take sleeping pills, sedatives, or illicit drugs, and I am not having withdrawal from anything.
I cut out coffee and try to exercise, but I have never taken prescription medication or seen a counselor for this before.
I thought maybe I was just naturally a chronic worrier, but lately it feels like it's taking over my daily life.
I'm really worried that I'll lose my temper with my family or mess up a big project at work because my head won't stop spinning.
I'd like to get my labs checked to make sure nothing physical is wrong and get some advice on how to shut my mind off at night.
I don't have any chronic illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart disease.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or nicotine products.
I only drink occasionally in social settings, maybe one beer a month, and I haven't had any alcohol recently.
I work in an office setting and live with my wife and child in an apartment.
There is no family history of thyroid disorders, heart problems, or major psychiatric conditions that I know of.
